message.content: {"passages":[{"reference":"1.9","text":"When I said, “I would like to meet one of those who have seen him,” they immediately led me, saying, “There is someone here who has not only met him personally but also comes from the land over there, a Hebrew man named Barnabas. He says that he himself is one of his disciples, and while sitting somewhere around here he readily tells anyone who wishes the words of his promise.” So I went with them. When I arrived, I stood with the crowd present, listening to his words, and I perceived that he was speaking the truth—not with dialectical technique, but guilelessly and without preparation setting out what he had heard and witnessed the Son of God who had appeared do and say. He also supplied many witnesses for the wonders and sayings of which he spoke, including people from the very crowd present.","lexical_decisions":[{"source_quote":"ἱστορήσας αὐτὸν","chosen":"met him personally","rationale":"ἱστορέω with a personal object can denote visiting or becoming personally acquainted with someone, not merely learning facts about him."},{"source_quote":"τῆς ἐκεῖθεν γῆς ὑπάρχων","chosen":"comes from the land over there","rationale":"Preserves the deliberately deictic description of Barnabas’s place of origin."},{"source_quote":"τῆς ἐκείνου ὑποσχέσεως τοὺς λόγους","chosen":"the words of his promise","rationale":"Retains the source’s ὑπόσχεσις language rather than replacing it with a more familiar theological term."},{"source_quote":"τὸν τοῦ θεοῦ φανέντα υἱὸν","chosen":"the Son of God who had appeared","rationale":"Treats φανέντα as modifying the Son and preserves the source’s claim without doctrinal expansion."},{"source_quote":"τῶν ὑπ᾽ αὐτοῦ λεγομένων θαυμασίων τε καὶ λόγων","chosen":"the wonders and sayings of which he spoke","rationale":"The phrase concerns the wonders and sayings being recounted by Barnabas; this wording avoids assigning every λόγος directly to an unstated speaker."}],"source_issues":[]},{"reference":"1.10","text":"Because the crowds were favorably disposed toward what was being said without cunning, the philosophers whose starting point was worldly education began laughing at him and mocking him, jeering and deriding him with boundless audacity, as though they were wielding syllogisms as mighty weapons. But he, fending off their nonsense, would not be drawn into their crafty questioning. Remaining undaunted, he did not stop speaking. Once someone asked him why a gnat had come into being and, though extremely tiny and having six feet, also has wings, while an elephant, the largest of animals, has only four feet and no wings. After the question, he took up the discourse that had been interrupted and, as though he had answered the question, resumed the discourse that had been set before him from the beginning, using only this preface after each interruption: “We are commanded only to tell you the words and wonderful deeds of the one who sent us, and instead of a logical demonstration we present to you many witnesses from among those of you who are here. I remember their forms as living images, sufficient testimonies. What remains is in your power: to yield or to disobey. But I will not cease telling you what benefits you, because for me silence is loss, while for you disobedience is harm. I could also give demonstrations in response to your speculative questions, if you asked in a truth-loving spirit. But now is not a suitable time to tell you the reason for the differing creation of the gnat and the elephant, when you are ignorant of the God of the universe.”","lexical_decisions":[{"source_quote":"οἱ ἐκ παιδείας κοσμικῆς ὁρμώμενοι φιλόσοφοι","chosen":"the philosophers whose starting point was worldly education","rationale":"ὁρμώμενοι identifies the basis from which they proceeded, while κοσμική retains the author’s contrast with the herald’s teaching."},{"source_quote":"οὐ συνέτρεχεν αὐτῶν τῇ πανούργῳ πεύσει","chosen":"would not be drawn into their crafty questioning","rationale":"The idiom conveys refusal to join or follow their line of questioning rather than inability to answer."},{"source_quote":"ὡς πρὸς τὴν πεῦσιν ἀποκρινάμενος","chosen":"as though he had answered the question","rationale":"ὡς marks the narrator’s comparison; the following preface functions as an indirect response rather than an explanation of the animals."},{"source_quote":"ὧν ἐγὼ τὰ εἴδη μέμνημαι ὡς ἐμψύχους εἰκόνας ἱκανὰς μαρτυρίας","chosen":"I remember their forms as living images, sufficient testimonies","rationale":"Preserves the unusual sequence of remembered forms, living images, and testimonies without reducing it to a generic claim that he recognized witnesses."},{"source_quote":"τῶν εἰκαίων ὑμῶν προβλημάτων","chosen":"your speculative questions","rationale":"εἰκαῖος points to matters based on probability or conjecture; the context presents them as proposed intellectual problems."},{"source_quote":"τοῖς τῶν ὅλων ἀγνοοῦσι θεόν","chosen":"when you are ignorant of the God of the universe","rationale":"The hyperbaton joins θεόν with τῶν ὅλων and addresses the hearers directly through the participle."}],"source_issues":[]},{"reference":"1.11","text":"As he was saying these things, they let loose disorderly laughter as though by agreement, trying to silence him and leave him at a loss, as if he were some demon-possessed barbarian. When I saw this, I was seized—I do not know how—by zeal, with pious indignation, and could no longer endure remaining silent. Instead, I cried out boldly: “God had good reason to make his will incomprehensible to you, since he foresaw that you were unworthy, as is evident from the things by which he now gives assurance to those who possess a discerning mind. For now heralds of his will have been sent out, not professing grammatical skill but disclosing his will in simple and guileless words, so that absolutely anyone who hears can understand what is said, and not with some grudging polish unwilling to make itself available to everyone. Yet you are here not only failing to understand what benefits you, but also, to your own harm, laughing at the truth that made its home among barbarians to your condemnation. Though it has now visited you as well, you do not wish to receive it as a guest, because of your licentiousness and the plainness of its words, lest you be exposed as lovers of words to no purpose and not philosophers who love truth. How long, then, will you go on learning to talk when you do not know how to speak well? Many words from you are not worth one reasoned statement. What, then, will your Greek multitude say, having become a single soul, if there really is to be a judgment, as this man says? ‘Why, O God, did you not proclaim your will to us?’ Will you not most certainly hear—if indeed you are deemed worthy of an answer—the following? ‘Knowing before the world’s foundation every choice that would be made, I secretly dealt with each person beforehand according to what that person deserved. Wishing to assure those who have taken refuge with me of precisely this—that it is so, and why from the beginning, in the earlier generations, I did not allow my will to be proclaimed publicly—I have now, near the end of life, sent heralds of my purpose. They are laughed at and, while being abused, are mocked by those unwilling to receive any benefit and who have vehemently rejected my friendship. Oh, what great injustice! The heralds are in danger even of being murdered, and that at the hands of the very people being called to salvation.’”","lexical_decisions":[{"source_quote":"ὡς βάρβαρόν τινα δαιμονῶντα","chosen":"as if he were some demon-possessed barbarian","rationale":"δαιμονάω can describe demonic possession or the madness attributed to it; the rendering preserves the explicit demonic characterization."},{"source_quote":"ἀναξίους προιδὼν ὡς ἐξ ὧν νῦν τοὺς κριτικὸν νοῦν ἔχοντας πληροφορῶν φαίνεται","chosen":"since he foresaw that you were unworthy, as is evident from the things by which he now gives assurance to those who possess a discerning mind","rationale":"The syntax is compressed; this rendering takes ἐξ ὧν with φαίνεται and God as the understood subject of πληροφορῶν."},{"source_quote":"ὡς πάνθ’ ὁντιναοῦν ἀκούσαντα νοεῖν τὰ λεγόμενα","chosen":"so that absolutely anyone who hears can understand what is said","rationale":"πάνθ’ reflects the aspirated elision of πάντα before ὁντιναοῦν and intensifies the unrestricted ‘anyone whatsoever.’"},{"source_quote":"ξέσεώς τινος φθονερᾶς","chosen":"some grudging polish","rationale":"ξέσις denotes polishing or refinement of expression, while φθονερά portrays such refinement as withholding accessibility from ordinary hearers."},{"source_quote":"τὴν εἰς τὴν ὑμετέραν καταδίκην ἐν βαρβάροις πολιτευσαμένην ἀλήθειαν","chosen":"the truth that made its home among barbarians to your condemnation","rationale":"πολιτεύομαι depicts truth as living or conducting its life among a people; the personified image is retained."},{"source_quote":"εἰκῇ φιλόλογοί ἐστε καὶ οὐ φιλαληθεῖς φιλόσοφοι","chosen":"lovers of words to no purpose and not philosophers who love truth","rationale":"Preserves the author’s contrast and wordplay between devotion to λόγοι and devotion to truth."},{"source_quote":"ἑκάστῳ πρὸς τὸ αὐτοῦ ἄξιον λανθανόντως προαπήντησα","chosen":"I secretly dealt with each person beforehand according to what that person deserved","rationale":"προαπαντάω literally suggests meeting in advance, but here describes prior, hidden treatment corresponding to each person’s deserts."},{"source_quote":"πρὸς τῷ τέλει τοῦ βίου","chosen":"near the end of life","rationale":"Retains βίος as ‘life’ rather than silently substituting the more familiar ‘end of the age’ or ‘end of the world.’"}],"source_issues":[]},{"reference":"1.12","text":"“‘This injustice being done against my heralds would have been done against all of them from the beginning, if the unworthy had been called to salvation from the beginning. For the injustice now being done by them serves as a defense of my just providence: I rightly did not wish from the beginning to expose publicly and to no benefit the message worthy of honor to abuse. Instead, I resolved that it should be kept silent as something precious—not from those who were worthy from the beginning, with whom I did share it, but from these and others like them, who, as you see, are unworthy, who hate me and are unwilling to love themselves.’ And now, stop laughing at this man and question me about what he proclaims; or let anyone willing answer me when I question him. Do not bark like wanton dogs, shutting the ears of those who wish to be saved with disorderly noise. You unjust people, hateful to God, who turn the reasoning that saves aside into unbelief—how can you obtain forgiveness when you insult the man who professes to tell you about the divinity of God? And you do this to a man whom, even if he were saying nothing true, you ought to have welcomed because of his good intention toward you.”","lexical_decisions":[{"source_quote":"εἰς ἀπολογίαν τῆς ἐμῆς δικαίας γίνεται προνοίας","chosen":"serves as a defense of my just providence","rationale":"ἀπολογία denotes a defense or vindication; the mistreatment of the heralds is presented as vindicating the prior withholding."},{"source_quote":"τὸν τιμῆς ἄξιον λόγον","chosen":"the message worthy of honor","rationale":"λόγος here refers to the proclaimed content; ‘message’ avoids importing a personified or canonical sense not required by the context."},{"source_quote":"σιγᾶσθαι αὐτὸν ὡς τίμιον","chosen":"that it should be kept silent as something precious","rationale":"The passive infinitive depicts the message as withheld, while τίμιος emphasizes its precious or honored status."},{"source_quote":"παρέντες· γελᾶν τὸν ἄνδρα τοῦτον","chosen":"stop laughing at this man","rationale":"Despite the printed medial punctuation, παρέντες governs the infinitive γελᾶν in the sense of leaving off or ceasing the action."},{"source_quote":"μύοντες τῶν σώζεσθαι θελόντων τὰς ἀκοάς","chosen":"shutting the ears of those who wish to be saved","rationale":"Preserves the bodily image of closing the hearers’ ears rather than generalizing it as mere interference."},{"source_quote":"θεοστυγεῖς","chosen":"hateful to God","rationale":"The adjective can be understood as hated by or hateful to God; the passive sense fits its coordination with the condemnatory vocative ἄδικοι."},{"source_quote":"τὸν σώζοντα λογισμὸν εἰς ἀπιστίαν ἀπασχολοῦντες","chosen":"who turn the reasoning that saves aside into unbelief","rationale":"ἀπασχολέω conveys occupying or diverting something; the rendering preserves both the saving function of the reasoning and its redirection toward unbelief."},{"source_quote":"τὴν θειότητα τοῦ θεοῦ","chosen":"the divinity of God","rationale":"Retains the source’s explicit and somewhat tautological wording without converting it into a more developed doctrinal formula."}],"source_issues":[]}]}
